entry: Fifth king of the Chakri dynasty of Siam (r. 1868–1910), titled Rama V. His reign brought the modernization of Siam, governmental and social reforms, and territorial concessions to the British and French empires, policies aimed at preserving Siam's independence amid European colonies. He was the son of King Mongkut, who prepared him for an innovative reign and had him educated in [[Buddhism]] and Pali, as well as science, English and French. In 1868 Mongkut and his son both contracted [[Malaria|malaria]] on an expedition to observe a solar eclipse, and Mongkut died in Bangkok on October 1, 1868. A council chose Chulalongkorn as successor; because he was 15, Sri Suriyawongse served as regent until he turned 20. In 1871 he visited Singapore and Java to study British colonial administration. He was given the epithet Phra Piya Maharat, the Great Beloved King.

1994 Hong Kong romantic anthology film written and directed by [[Wong Kar-wai]]. Its two stories follow lovesick Hong Kong policemen, played by Takeshi Kaneshiro and Tony Leung. The title refers to Chungking Mansions in Tsim Sha Tsui, where much of the first story takes place. The film premiered in Hong Kong on July 14, 1994. It is regarded as a major work of Hong Kong cinema and as one of Wong's most significant works. In 2022 it ranked 88th in the *Sight and Sound* decennial critics' poll of the greatest films.

Legendary creature of folklore in the Americas, said to prey on [[Livestock|livestock]], especially goats. Its name means 'goat-sucker' in Spanish. Accounts say it kills by puncturing the neck and draining its victims' blood, an association that gave rise to its link with vampirism. Descriptions vary by region: in [[Puerto Rico]] it is often reptilian with a row of spines, while reports from the Southwestern United States describe a hairless canine. The first widely publicized sightings took place in Puerto Rico in 1995. Investigations of purported sightings in northern [[Mexico]] and the Southern United States identified canids afflicted by severe mange.

Building used for Christian worship and related religious activities. The word derives from Old English *cirice*, from Ancient Greek *kyriakon*, meaning 'of the Lord'. The earliest identified church is the Dura-Europos house church, founded between AD 233 and 256. Purpose-built halls for worship began to be constructed in the late third century, and larger churches appeared under [[Constantine the Great|Emperor Constantine]]. Many churches follow a cross-shaped plan, in which the central aisle and seating form the vertical beam and the [[Altar|altar]] area forms the horizontal. Steeples often house bells. From the 11th to the 14th century a wave of cathedral and parish church construction swept [[Western Europe]]. Several churches are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Established Christian church in England and the Crown Dependencies, and the initial church of the Anglican tradition. In 1534 it renounced papal authority under [[Henry VIII]], beginning the English Reformation. [[Thomas Cranmer|Thomas Cranmer]] developed its liturgy, including the *Book of Common Prayer*. The Elizabethan Settlement (1559–1563) under [[Elizabeth I]] set the church on a middle course, a via media, between Lutheranism and Calvinism. The reigning monarch is its Supreme Governor, and the Archbishop of Canterbury is its most senior cleric. Its General Synod passes measures that must be approved by the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament of the United Kingdom]].

Fourth-century church in Jerusalem's Old City, traditionally identified as the site of the [[Crucifixion of Jesus|crucifixion]] of [[Jesus]] and his empty tomb. Built under [[Constantine the Great]] after the tomb was rediscovered around 325, it was destroyed in 1009 and rebuilt, with completion in 1048. Crusaders captured it in 1099 and modified it further. The church is the seat of the Armenian, Greek Orthodox and Catholic Latin patriarchates of Jerusalem. Control is shared among several Christian denominations under the Status Quo, an understanding dating to 1757. Its original Greek name was Church of the Anastasis (Resurrection), and it has been a major Christian pilgrimage destination since its creation.

American professional wrestler, bodybuilder and actress. Billed as "The Ninth Wonder of the World," she rose to prominence in the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE) in 1997 as a member of the stable D-Generation X. She held the WWF Intercontinental Championship twice and the WWF Women's Championship once, and was the first woman to participate in the Royal Rumble match. She left the WWF in 2001. Outside wrestling she appeared twice in *Playboy* and on television, including *The Surreal Life*. She was posthumously inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2019.

Insect of the superfamily Cicadoidea, order [[Hemiptera]]. Cicadas produce an exceptionally loud song by rapidly buckling and unbuckling drum-like tymbals. Most species are annual, emerging as adults every year, and more than 3,000 species have been described. The North American genus *Magicicada*, the periodical cicadas, spends most of its life underground as nymphs and emerges in synchronized masses every 13 or 17 years, which may reduce predation by overwhelming predators with sheer numbers. Cicadas cannot bite or sting and are harmless to humans. They are eaten in China, Myanmar, Malaysia, central Africa and parts of Mexico.

Member of a large, diverse family of percomorph fish, Cichlidae. At least 1,760 species have been scientifically described, making it one of the largest vertebrate families; only the Cyprinidae have more species. Cichlids are native to the Neotropics, Africa including Madagascar, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent. They have undergone rapid evolution into diverse species flocks in the African Great Lakes, which is important for the study of speciation. Many species are important food fishes, such as [[Tilapia|tilapia]], and many are popular aquarium fish, including angelfish, oscars and discus. Cichlids have the largest number of [[Endangered species|endangered]] species among vertebrate families. All practice some form of parental care, usually guarding eggs and fry or mouthbrooding.

Alcoholic beverage made by fermenting the juice of [[Apple|apples]]. Most apple varieties, including crab apples, can be used, but cider apples are most desirable. Sugar or extra fruit added before a second fermentation increases the alcohol content. Cider is especially popular in Britain, particularly the West Country, and in [[Ireland]], which together have the world's highest per capita consumption. It was widely consumed in England by the 11th century. European settlers introduced apple cultivation for cider to North America in the 17th century, where it became a staple of colonial New England and Virginia. Its popularity declined in the 19th century under the Temperance Movement and was further suppressed by Prohibition in the 1920s. In the United States, sales have more than doubled since 2015, reaching an estimated $603 million in 2025.

Thin cylinder of tobacco rolled in paper for smoking. Cigarette smoking is the most common method of tobacco consumption. [[Nicotine]], the psychoactive drug in tobacco, makes cigarettes highly addictive. Smoke contains over 7,000 chemicals, at least 70 of them known carcinogens. Smoking causes diseases including [[Cancer|cancer]], [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease|chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] and heart disease, and it causes more than 8 million deaths worldwide each year, including more than 1.3 million non-smokers exposed to secondhand smoke. About half of smokers die of tobacco-related disease, losing an average of 14 years of life. [[Electronic cigarette|Electronic cigarettes]], developed in the 21st century, are considered less harmful but still carry significant risks. Legislation has restricted smoking in public places, regulated marketing and raised taxes.

Single-celled [[Protist|protist]] of the phylum Ciliophora, characterized by hair-like organelles called cilia. Cilia are structurally identical to flagella but are shorter and more numerous. They are used for swimming, crawling, attachment, feeding and sensation. About 4,500 free-living species have been described, and the potential number of extant species is estimated at 27,000–40,000. Ciliates range in size from 10 μm to 4 mm and are common in lakes, ponds, oceans and wet soils. Most are free-living or commensal, but some are parasites, including *Balantidium coli*, the only ciliate known to infect humans. Reproduction is by binary fission or conjugation, and contractile vacuoles regulate osmotic balance in freshwater habitats.

City in Hamilton County, southwestern Ohio, on the [[Ohio River]] opposite Kentucky. Settled in 1788, Cincinnati was among the top 10 U.S. cities by population for much of the 19th century. As an inland port for steamboats, it was also a hub of Underground Railroad activity. Its population was 309,317 at the 2020 census. In the late 19th century it was called the "Paris of America" for its architecture. Its major league teams include the Cincinnati Reds (Major League Baseball) and the Bengals ([[National Football League|NFL]]). The city is home to the University of Cincinnati and the seat of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

Folk tale with variants told throughout the world. Its protagonist, a young girl in unfortunate circumstances, is blessed with remarkable fortune and rises to the throne through marriage. The first literary Western version was Giambattista Basile's "La Gatta Cenerentola," published posthumously in his *Pentamerone* in 1634. The version best known in English was published by [[Charles Perrault]] as *Cendrillon* in 1697, which introduced the fairy godmother, the pumpkin carriage and the glass slipper. The [[Brothers Grimm]] published *Aschenputtel* in 1812. Disney's 1950 animated feature popularized the tale in the 20th century. The word Cinderella has come to mean someone who unexpectedly achieves success after a period of obscurity.

American model, actress and entrepreneur. One of the most popular supermodels of the 1980s and 1990s, she appeared on magazine covers, runways and fashion campaigns, including advertisements for [[Pepsi]] and Revlon. She won the Elite Look of the Year award at age 17. Crawford acted in films such as *Fair Game* (1995) and later built a business in skincare. Her line Meaningful Beauty, developed with dermatologist Dr. Jean-Louis Sebagh, had annual sales exceeding $100 million. She married businessman Rande Gerber in 1998; their children, Presley and Kaia Gerber, have also become models.

Film industry of mainland China, one of three historical threads of Chinese-language cinema, with those of Hong Kong and Taiwan. Foreign films were screened from 1896, and the first domestic feature, *Dingjun Mountain*, was produced in 1905. After the 1949 communist victory, film production was nationalized and focused on propaganda, nearly ceasing during the [[Cultural Revolution]] (1966–1976). Economic reforms after 1978 brought the Fifth Generation directors, including Zhang Yimou and Chen Kaige, whose films such as *Red Sorghum* (1987) won international acclaim. Box office receipts peaked at over 64 billion yuan in 2019 before declining to 42.5 billion yuan in 2024. Films remain subject to pre-approval by the National Radio and Television Administration, and [[Censorship|censorship]] shapes content.

Film industry of France and the film productions of French companies abroad. It is the oldest and largest precursor of national cinemas in Europe. The Lumière brothers launched cinematography in 1895 with *L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat*. By the early 1900s French cinema led globally, and [[Georges Méliès|Méliès]] made *A Trip to the Moon* (1902). After World War I, U.S. films flooded Europe and French cinema declined, prompting import quotas. The New Wave of the late 1950s and 1960s, led by [[Jean-Luc Godard]] and [[François Truffaut]], produced *Breathless* (1960) and *The 400 Blows* (1959). In 2013 France was the second-largest exporter of films after the United States. The Centre national du cinéma et de l'image animée (CNC), founded in 1946, regulates and funds the sector through levies on tickets. French films have won 12 Academy Awards for Best International Feature Film, second only to Italy's 14.

Motion pictures produced by the Indian film industry, which is made up of many industries working in different languages. India has no single national film industry; films are made in [[Hindi]], Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Bengali and other languages. Major production centers include [[Mumbai]], [[Hyderabad]], [[Chennai]] and [[Kolkata]]. The industry has ranked first in the world in annual film output for a number of years. [[Dadasaheb Phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]]'s *Raja Harishchandra* (1913) is recognized as India's first full-length feature film. As of 2022 Telugu cinema sold 23.3 crore (233 million) tickets, followed by Tamil with 20.5 crore (205 million) and Hindi with 18.9 crore (189 million). Ramoji Film City in Hyderabad, measuring over 1,666 acres (674 ha), is certified by [[Guinness World Records|Guinness World Records]] as the largest film studio complex in the world.

Film industry of Japan, one of the world's oldest, which began in the late 1890s. In 2022 Japan was the fourth-largest producer of feature films (634) and the third-largest by box office revenue ($1.5 billion). In the 1950s, a period known as the "Golden Age" of Japanese cinema, the jidaigeki films of [[Akira Kurosawa]] and the science-fiction films of Ishirō Honda and Eiji Tsuburaya gained international praise. Kurosawa's *Seven Samurai* (1954) topped the BBC's 2018 survey of the 100 greatest foreign-language films. Japan has won five [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best International Feature Film, more than any other Asian country. [[Anime|Anime]] rose in popularity in the 1980s, and Studio Ghibli's *Princess Mononoke* (1997) and *Spirited Away* (2001) are among its highest-grossing films. As of 2025, the top 16 highest-grossing Japanese films worldwide are all anime.

State-controlled film industry of the Soviet Union, from the 1920s to 1991. Films were made by the constituent republics under central regulation in Moscow, most prolifically the Russian republic, followed by Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Ukraine. After the 1917 [[Russian Revolution|Bolshevik Revolution]], [[Vladimir Lenin]] prioritized cinema as a tool of mass propaganda. [[Sergei Eisenstein]] and Dziga Vertov pioneered montage editing, and Eisenstein's *Battleship Potemkin* (1925) became a propaganda triumph and an influential work of film theory. Under Stalin the industry enforced socialist realism. Thaws under Khrushchev and Brezhnev allowed more personal work, such as [[Andrei Tarkovsky]]'s *Andrei Rublev* (1966). Output peaked at around 50 features a year.

Motion picture industry of the United States, centered in Hollywood, California. It has influenced the global film industry since the early 20th century. In 1894 the first commercial motion-picture exhibition took place in New York City, using [[Thomas Edison]]'s kinetoscope. The United States produced the first sync-sound musical film, *The Jazz Singer* (1927). By the early 1920s the industry was the world's film capital, dominated by studios such as MGM, Warner Bros. and Paramount. In 2024 the United States produced 544 national feature films, the fourth-largest total after India, Japan and China. The New Hollywood of the 1970s brought auteurs such as [[Steven Spielberg]] and [[Martin Scorsese]]. [[Orson Welles|Orson Welles]]'s *Citizen Kane* (1941) is frequently cited in critics' polls as the greatest film of all time.

Art of motion picture photography, including electronic video photography. A cinematographer uses a [[Lens|lens]] to focus reflected light onto an image sensor or light-sensitive film, and exposures are recorded in sequence. On film they form latent images that are chemically developed; electronic sensors produce an electrical charge for each pixel, which is stored as video. The field took shape in the late 19th century. [[Eadweard Muybridge|Eadweard Muybridge]] made sequential photographs of animal locomotion in 1878, and in 1895 the [[Lumière brothers|Lumière brothers]] introduced the Cinematographe, a portable device for filming, printing and projecting. The Steadicam, introduced in 1975, allowed fluid tracking shots. Beginning in the late 1990s, electronic sensors began replacing chemical film stocks.

Red mercury(II) sulfide mineral, HgS. It is the most common ore for refining elemental [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] and the historical source of the scarlet pigment [[Vermilion|vermilion]]. Cinnabar generally occurs as a vein-filling mineral associated with volcanic activity and alkaline hot springs. Its Mohs hardness is between 2.0 and 2.5, and its specific gravity is approximately 8.1. It was used as a pigment since antiquity in the Near East, the New World and China, where it was applied to stoneware as early as the Yangshao culture. Because its mercury content is toxic, handling it requires precautions, a risk recognized as early as ancient Rome.

Spice obtained from the inner bark of several *Cinnamomum* tree species. It is used mainly as an aromatic condiment and flavoring in sweet and savory dishes, including biscuits, breakfast cereals, teas and hot chocolate. Its aroma comes from its essential oil, principally cinnamaldehyde. *Cinnamomum verum*, known as Ceylon cinnamon, is native to [[Sri Lanka|Sri Lanka]], but most commercial cinnamon is cassia from four other species, such as *C. cassia* (Chinese cinnamon). Ceylon cinnamon contains approximately 0.004% coumarin, while cassia contains approximately 1%, a level that can cause liver and kidney damage with regular large consumption. In 2023 world production was 238,403 tonnes, led by [[China|China]] with 39% of the total.

Natural oscillation that repeats roughly every 24 hours. Circadian rhythms originate within an organism and are adjusted to the environment by external cues called zeitgebers, such as light and temperature. They are regulated by a circadian clock that coordinates biological processes so they occur at the correct time. Circadian rhythms have been observed in animals, plants, fungi and [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]], and appear to have evolved independently in each kingdom. The term comes from the Latin *circa*, 'around', and *dies*, 'day'. Disruption from shift work or jet lag is linked to increased risks of [[Obesity|obesity]] and [[Diabetes|diabetes]].
